11.0.s.en: (1) The dispute over the acceptance of the Gentiles

11.0.0.en: The word of God: faith in Christ.

11.0.1.en: The rest of the Fathers the Apostles, members of the Mother Church in Jerusalem, heard of what had been done through Peter in the acceptance of the Gentiles, and this was not easy for them to accept.

11.1.0.en: They that were of the circumcision: the Christians who had converted from Jewish origin.

11.1.1.en: Men uncircumcised: not circumcised, that is, Gentiles.

11.1.2.en: When Peter went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem, the Christians of Jewish origin objected to him strongly because of his mixing with the Gentiles, for this was against the Law of Moses.

11.2.0.en: Peter began to relate to them what had happened in order, to prove to them that the One who made the decision in that acceptance was God and not he.

11.3.0.en: Peter told them of his vision on the housetop in Joppa, where he saw the sheet coming down from heaven containing the animals, and God commanded him to eat of them because they are all clean, for they are God’s creation.

11.4.0.en: Peter objected because he did not eat the forbidden animals, so God confirmed their cleanness to him three times. Thus the symbols of the Jewish Law come to an end as the New Covenant begins.

11.5.0.en: Peter connected the vision with the arrival of the messengers of Cornelius immediately after it.

11.6.1.en: The Holy Spirit commanded Peter to go with them without doubting the clear meaning of the vision, and he took with him six of the Christians of Joppa to testify before them to the truth of what had happened.

11.7.0.en: Their entering the house of Cornelius was a fulfillment of the command of the angel who had appeared to him, and not of their own personal opinion, in order to preach to them, great and small, the message of salvation.

11.8.0.en: The beginning: the day of Pentecost, when the Church began with the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples who were gathered.

11.8.1.en: The descent of the Holy Spirit upon the hearers during Peter’s speech was proof of the acceptance of the Gentiles, so Peter remembered the words of Christ about the baptism of believers in the New Testament with the Holy Spirit.

11.9.0.en: The gift: the descent of the Holy Spirit and His gifts.

11.9.1.en: Could I withstand God: could I withstand God’s command to accept them into the faith, baptize them and mingle with them? If this was God’s decision, then no man, whoever he may be, is able to withstand God.

11.10.0.en: They held their peace: they were convinced and no longer had any argument or objection with which to dispute.

11.10.1.en: They glorified God: a proof of complete conviction and then of rejoicing in the work of God.

11.10.2.en: Unto life: in the faith as members of the Church, and then the inheritance of eternal life.

11.10.3.en: The Church of Jerusalem was convinced and ceased from disputing, in submission to God’s command, and they began to glorify Him because He had accepted the Gentiles without circumcision.

11.10.4.en: Submit to the words of the Holy Bible and the teachings of the Church even if your mind does not grasp them, and then God will convince you because of your love and obedience to Him; and be diligent to carry out His word and to repent that you may enjoy life with Him.

11.11.s.en: (2) The extension of the ministry to Antioch

11.11.0.en: Phenice: the meaning of its name is “land of palms,” and it is present-day Lebanon, and its most important cities are Tyre and Sidon on the Mediterranean Sea.

11.11.1.en: Cyprus: a fertile island in the Mediterranean Sea, now written (Cyprus). Antioch: it lies on the Orontes River in present-day Syria, and was built in 301 B.C. by the Greek Seleucids and named after Antiochus. It is considered the capital of the Church of the Gentile Christians, just as Jerusalem was the capital of the Church of the Christians of Jewish origin, and it was considered the third greatest city in the world among the Romans after Rome and Alexandria.

11.11.2.en: The believers, except the Apostles, were scattered from Jerusalem after the persecution that began with the killing of Stephen, and these believers moved to Phenicia, Cyprus and Antioch. They were preaching only to the Jews of their own nation.

11.12.0.en: Some Jews of Cypriot origin and from North Africa (Cyrene) were less fanatical than the Jews of Palestine, and when they reached Antioch they dared to preach Christ among the pagan Greeks, and God supported them in their preaching, so many believed.

11.13.0.en: The tidings: that is, the spread of the faith not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles in Antioch.

11.13.1.en: This news reached the Church of Jerusalem, so they sent Barnabas, who was a powerful preacher and teacher, to Antioch to help in the ministry, especially since he was Cypriot by origin and would be more acceptable to the Cypriots.

11.14.0.en: Full of the Holy Ghost: a good vessel in whom the Holy Spirit works with power in good works and effective preaching.

11.14.1.en: Barnabas came to Antioch and rejoiced over the new believers there, and exhorted them to stand firm in the faith with power; and because he was a good and wise man, this helped in spreading the good news and increasing the number of believers.

11.15.0.en: The Apostle Paul was at that time in an unknown place in the city of Tarsus, which lies in Cilicia in Turkey, so Barnabas saw fit to have him share with him in the ministry of Antioch, because they had served together before in Jerusalem (ch. 9:27).

11.16.0.en: Barnabas and Paul continued serving for a year in Antioch, and about ten years had passed since the crucifixion of Christ, and the good news had spread that made clear that Jesus is the Christ, so the believers were called Christians for the first time, after Christ the Redeemer. This shows us that the person of Christ was the center of the life of the believers and of the Church in Antioch at that time.

11.17.0.en: Prophets from Jerusalem: Christians from Jerusalem who prophesy. The Lord sent to the Church of Antioch believers who had the gift of prophecy.

11.18.0.en: These believers prophesied that a great gathering would occur in the world, and this was fulfilled in A.D. 44 in the days of the Roman emperor Claudius.

11.19.0.en: Determined: the leaders of the Church in Antioch decided and commanded that gifts must be collected for the poor Christians of Jerusalem.

11.19.1.en: The disciples: the Christians, the believing disciples of Christ in Antioch.

11.19.2.en: According to his ability: according to the capacity of each person and his financial means.

11.19.5.en: The love of the Church of Antioch appeared immediately, so they collected what could be collected to help the believers of Judea, whom the Jews were persecuting and whose property they often confiscated.

11.20.0.en: They sent what they had collected with Barnabas and Saul to Jerusalem. It is noticed that at this time Barnabas was named before Saul.

11.20.1.en: The offering reached the leaders of the Church of Jerusalem, whether apostles, bishops or priests, whom the Scripture calls the elders.

11.20.2.en: Barnabas was a great man of wide heart, who loved to share the ministry with others and not to confine it to himself, and even his possessions he had sold earlier and given to the Apostles (ch. 4:37). May God give us breadth of heart and love, which is the greatest of the virtues, so that we care to give to everyone in need, and share with those around us in working with us, putting them forward in honor so that they may be encouraged and rejoice in serving God. The martyrdom of James and the imprisonment and deliverance of Peter

12.0.s.en: (1) The killing of James and the arrest of Peter

12.0.0.en: About that time: about A.D. 44, the time of the arrival of Barnabas and Saul with gifts for the poor Christians of Jerusalem.

12.0.1.en: Certain: some of the believers from among the ordinary members of the Church.

12.0.2.en: Herod: a name repeated in the Holy Bible. The first was Herod the Great (Mt 2:1-3), the killer of the children of Bethlehem, who killed his son Aristobulus. The second Herod is the killer of the Baptist (Mk 6:14), and the third Herod is the killer of the Apostle James (ch. 12:1-2), the brother of Herodias and son of Aristobulus, nephew of the second Herod and grandson of Herod the Great; he was called Herod Agrippa I, and his mother was Jewish.

12.0.3.en: Herod Agrippa began the persecution of the Christians in Jerusalem, and that was at the time of the arrival of Barnabas and Saul with gifts for the needy believers in Jerusalem.

12.0.4.en: This was the first Roman persecution of the early Church, because the previous persecutions were all Jewish.

12.1.0.en: James the Apostle: one of the three who were closer to Christ than the rest of the twelve Apostles.

12.1.1.en: The brother of John: the Book of Acts was written after the death of James, and his brother John was still alive and well known, so it said “the brother of John.”

12.1.2.en: Herod seized James and killed him, thereby trying to win the Jews, and he cut off his head with the sword, as his uncle had done with John the Baptist.

12.1.3.en: Thus James drank of the cup as Christ had said to him (Mt 20:22), when his mother came asking a place for him at the right hand of the Lord.

12.2.0.en: It pleased the Jews: in order to secure his kingdom, because he was an intruder upon the Jews, so he tried to please them by persecuting the Christians, whom the Jews hated because of their growth and their changing the customs of the Jews. Peter: one of the well-known leaders of the Christians, so Herod tried to kill him as he had James, in order to destroy the strength of the Christians by killing their leaders.

12.2.1.en: Herod wished to kill Peter, so he arrested him, and that was in the seven days of unleavened bread following the feast of the Passover.

12.3.0.en: Four quaternions: each made up of four soldiers, two of them each bound to one of Peter’s hands and two guarding the door of the prison, and they were changed every three hours throughout the day, that is, four times, and this was repeated also at night.

12.3.1.en: To bring him forth: not for trial but for killing, like James.

12.3.2.en: Herod ordered that Peter be kept in prison under strict guard until the holy days of unleavened bread, on which killing is not permitted, were over, so that he might kill him after them. This shows Herod’s concern for the customs of the Jews in order to please them.

12.4.0.en: Without ceasing: this shows how great the Church’s love for Peter was and its strong faith in God, who is able to rescue him. The Church had regained its composure after recovering from the sudden shock of the killing of the Apostle James, so it was raising prayers to God to rescue Peter. For the Church has no power with which to face the world except the power of prayer.

12.4.1.en: Do not be disturbed by the violence of others’ wrongs against you, but lift your heart in prayer, confident of the power of God that supports you; for though He allows some trials for your benefit, He is able to stop the wrongs of others, and He cares greatly about your prayer because He loves you and is able to protect you.

12.5.0.en: Sleeping: this was at the end of the night, that is, the fourth watch, because the guard soldiers change every three hours and did not know that Peter was not there until the morning (v. 18), so it was in the last shift of the watch, which is before dawn.

12.5.1.en: The Lord waited, in His providence, until the night before the day when Herod was about to kill Peter, and Peter was deeply asleep in peace and complete trust in God; he was bound to two soldiers by both hands, while the other two soldiers were guarding the door.

12.6.1.en: God sent the angel to bring Peter out of the prison instead of the soldiers who were leading him to be killed, so the light of God shone in the place, and the angel struck the side of Peter, who was deeply asleep, to wake him, then called him to rise quickly, so that he would not doubt what he saw, and he rose to go out of the prison; and the chains of his hands fell off by themselves without the two soldiers noticing.

12.7.0.en: The angel asked Peter to put on his clothes and his sandals quietly and follow him, and Peter thought that he was in a vision.

12.8.0.en: The angel passed with Peter the first guard post and then the second, since he was confined in the inner prison, then they came to the outer gate, which also opened by itself in complete quiet, and when they had gone out of the prison the angel went with him along one of the streets of the city, then disappeared from him so that he could complete his way to the house.

12.9.0.en: Was come to himself: he became fully alert and realized what had happened to him.

12.9.1.en: Of a surety: he was certain that God had brought him out of the prison and rescued him from death. The expectation of the people of the Jews: who hated him and wanted to be rid of him. Here Peter realized the truth of his deliverance by the angel from the hand of Herod and the Jews.

12.10.0.en: When he had considered the thing: aware of all that had happened to him.

12.10.1.en: The house of Mary: it was the meeting place of Christ with His disciples, where He ate the Lord’s Supper and appeared to them after His resurrection, and where the Apostles were accustomed to gather.

12.10.2.en: John, whose surname was Mark: John is his Jewish name and Mark is his Greek name, and it was customary for a person to have two names in those times.

12.10.3.en: Praying: that God would rescue Peter.

12.10.4.en: The porch: the passage that leads to the outer door of the house.

12.10.5.en: Peter came to the house of St. Mark, where the believers were gathered for prayer all night, and when the maid “Rhoda” came to find out who was knocking at this hour, and recognized Peter’s voice, she was overwhelmed with joy so that she did not open the door but went back inside to tell those gathered of the miracle.

12.11.0.en: Thou art mad: her mind has become disordered and she is speaking untrue words.

12.11.1.en: Constantly affirmed: she was aware and certain that the voice was the voice of Peter, whom she knew well because of his frequent visits to this house.

12.11.2.en: Here we see something strange: the praying believers had faith in the power of prayer, but it was not enough to believe the answer; and since the believers held that each person has a guardian angel, they accused the maid of raving, supposing that the one standing at the door was Peter’s guardian angel who had come to comfort them.

12.12.0.en: Peter continued knocking, so they opened and were astonished when they saw him.

12.13.0.en: Peter asked them to be quiet and told them the story of his coming out of the prison, and asked them to inform James the Less the Apostle (the son of Alphaeus), one of the twelve, because he was the bishop of Jerusalem, and likewise to inform the rest of the believers of what had happened. And he went out to another place to hide there from the spies of King Herod.

12.14.0.en: No small stir: not only because of Peter’s disappearance, but because they expected severe punishment from Herod that might reach the point of killing them.

12.14.1.en: What was become: how Peter had disappeared, because they had not felt him go out and there were no traces showing how he got out of the prison.

12.14.2.en: When the sun rose, the soldiers were greatly disturbed because they did not find Peter in the prison.

12.15.0.en: Examined: he questioned the guards to learn how Peter escaped from the prison.

12.15.1.en: Should be put to death: when he failed to learn which of them had helped Peter escape, he ordered them to be killed for not keeping Peter, who escaped from them.

12.15.2.en: Caesarea: a great city in Judea on the coast of the Mediterranean, in which the force of the Roman authority was stationed.

12.15.3.en: Herod did not find Peter to kill him, so he ordered the soldiers to be killed, because Roman law decreed that the guard should suffer the punishment that would have befallen the one he was guarding if he escaped from him.

12.15.4.en: After that Herod left Jerusalem and came to Caesarea, where he stayed for the remainder of his life, which was very short.

12.15.5.en: God’s arrangements, for the course of events is not by the mere effort of man but by God, who permits and arranges everything according to His divine plan; so Peter was delivered and Herod is the one now about to die. Do not be disturbed if the wicked rise up against you or the events of the world press in on you, because God is able to rescue you from them and to change all the events around you.

12.16.0.en: Them of Tyre and Sidon: the people of Tyre and Sidon, which are cities on the coast of the Mediterranean in present-day Lebanon.

12.16.1.en: With one accord: it seems they were not in agreement, but out of fear of poverty and hunger they agreed to win Herod’s favor so that he would restore trade with them.

12.16.2.en: The king’s chamberlain: the one responsible for his palace and its guarding, who is of course trusted by the king and close to him.

12.16.3.en: Their country was nourished by the king’s country: it depended on trade with the lands subject to Herod.

12.16.4.en: Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon because of their commercial competition with the city of Caesarea, and they found that they had to appease him because of their great need to deal with the lands of Judea, since their land was commercial and not agricultural, and they were also small cities in which living required trading with Judea.

12.17.0.en: A set day: one of the feast days of Caesarea on the occasion of its founding.

12.17.1.en: When Herod put on his shining, splendid royal robe and sat on his throne in pride, addressing them with a pardon for them, these pagans began to flatter him, regarding him as a god and not a man.

12.18.0.en: Herod’s heart was lifted up and he believed the praise of the Tyrians that he was a god, and he did not give the glory to God, the Creator of all, so He struck him with worms to eat his flesh while he was alive, which is a matter of the utmost difficulty and pain, so he died a very horrible death, at the age of 54, in the fourth year of his reign.

12.19.0.en: The word of God: the preaching of Christ.

12.19.1.en: Here we come to the close of the chapter that began with the killing of James and the imprisonment of Peter, to see the death of Herod and the spread and growth of the preaching.

12.20.0.en: Ministry: delivering the gifts of the Church of Antioch to the needy among the believers in the Church of Jerusalem.

12.20.1.en: After Paul and Barnabas had been present at these events in Jerusalem, they returned to Antioch and took with them John (St. Mark), the son of Barnabas’s sister.

12.20.2.en: Do not be proud, however great your strength or authority, for God is longsuffering and able to punish the wicked, but He is patient with them that they may repent. So be humble, and do not be troubled because of your weakness, confident of the power of God that supports you; for as He supported the early Church, He is ready to uphold you with His grace and satisfy you with His love.

12.20.3.en: Barnabas and Paul on the first journey
